frontmatter.name: untangle-codebase
frontmatter.description: Untangle a whole codebase in one pass, so agents working in it read less per change, break less without noticing, and debug faster.

skills.excerpt: --- name: untangle-codebase description: Untangle a whole codebase in one pass, so agents working in it read less per change, break less without noticing, and debug faster. disable-model-invocation: true argument-hint: "[optional area or concern to focus on]" --- Start a thorough refactor of this codebase and complete it to the end. Treat this as a goal. **Why do this at all?** - **Better output:** agents write better code in a well-structured codebase. - **Cheaper & faster changes:** agents spend fewer tokens searching and more on the problem. - **Fewer silent breaks:** agents break less without noticing. - **Faster debugging:** agents find root causes faster. **1. Ask** Besides untangling the codebase, there are two other things you may do: | Addition | What it does | | --- | --- | | **Comments** | Remove comments that only restate the code. | | **Tests** | Remove tests that wouldn't catch a real bug, and fix the ones that fail without one. | List these (with their exact descriptions) for the user and ask which ones to do. Then do only those. **2. List every problem** Don't change anything yet. Go through the codebase asking one thing: **should these pieces change together?** Write down every place the code gets the answer wrong, as in the [decision log example](#decision-log-example). There are only three ways to get it wrong. **Hidden links:** pieces that must change together, where the code doesn't show it. - Copies of logic or values: change one and the others must change too, but nothing says so. - A module that reads a global or file set by another module: change that module and this one breaks, but nothing shows it (self-contained code). - A feature split across folders by layer, or related code in different folders: one change needs all of them, but the layout hides that (domain-driven code, colocation). - A call order or convention callers just have to know: change it and callers break, but nothing warns them (explicit over implicit). **Needless links:** pieces tied together that change for different reasons. - Callers that depend on internals: the internals change for their own reasons, and the callers break anyway (encapsulation). - Stable code that imports something more volatile: the stable code has to change whenever the volatile code does (dependency direction). - A general function with a parameter only one workflow understands: the function has to change whenever that workflow does (caller vocabulary). - A shallow module: its interface changes whenever its internals do, so its callers change with it (deep modules). **Surplus:** pieces with no reason of their own to change. - Wrappers: they only change when the thing they wrap does (pass-through wrappers). - Extension points and config for things that never vary: nothing will ever change them (speculative generality). - Dead code: nothing uses it, so nothing will ever need it to change. Also write down every **special case**: code that exists for one situation instead of following from how the system works. Each one is a requirement the design never accounted for, so use them to work out what the system needs to be. - An `if` for one value - A parameter for a specific caller - A swallowed exception - A retry or sleep - A disabled test **3. Redesign from first principles** Work out the fixes as if the system had known today's requirements from the start. Look for the one fix behind several problems, which often looks nothing like them. Don't fix special cases one by one. Ask the same thing of every fix, even one that looks better in the code: pieces that change together end up together, pieces that don't aren't tied, and everything depends on what changes less. Write each fix above the problems it solves, as in the [decision log example](#decision-log-example). **4. Fix everything on the list** Remove the special cases the redesign makes unnecessary, and keep the ones the system still needs. Don't go looking for bugs separately. A structural fix may fix some along the way, which is fine. If the user chose Comments: - Comments that restate the implementation, like `// sort first so the binary search works`, only change when it does, so they have no reason of their own to change. Remove them, even if they're phrased as a why. - Comments about something outside the code, like `// the proxy drops websockets, so we poll`, change when that does, and the code can't show it. Keep them. - Comments that explain a workaround om the codebase, like `// wait 100ms because the cache isn't ready yet`, only change when the problem behind the workaround does. They go when the redesign removes that problem. If the user chose Tests, do this last, because tests are your regression safety net. A test should fail on a regression, and only then: - Tests that repeat the implementation only change when it does, so they have no reason of their own to change. They check the same interpretation against itself, so remove them. - Tests tied to internals break when the code changes but behavior doesn't, so they change for the wrong reason. Rewrite them to depend on behavior, which changes less. - Tests that can't fail pass whatever the code does, so no change ever affects them. They aren't checking anything, so remove them. **5. Check, and repeat until done** Have subagents search for special cases, hidden links, needless links and surplus. **Do not stop until there is nothing worth fixing left.** You're done when: - **As few special cases are left in the system as possible.** How many remain is the best measure of how close you are. - A typical change lands in one place. - Every import is reasonable, and nothing imports anything more volatile than itself. - Subagents have no issues left that are worth fixing. - Intended behavior is the same as when you started, apart from bugs the refactor fixed. Test this at the end. **Tips** - **Start from a skeleton:** script away the function bodies, so the whole codebase fits in context. - **Summarize with subagents:** have them summarize parts of the codebase, so you can reason across all of it at once. - **Check the dependency graph often:** script one that shows what imports what, and rerun it as you go. - **Enter where leverage is highest:** start looking there first. - **Keep a decision log:** compaction is less of a problem that way. - **Use Git as evidence:** for how often pieces change, and what changes together. **Decision log example** The list of problems: ```md - `ui/LogoutDialog.tsx:30` waits 100ms after closing and hopes the message input can take focus by then. - `ui/Toolbar.tsx:40` and `ui/Menu.tsx:22` call the same actions, each with its own check for when they're disabled. - `checkout/submit.ts:9` depends directly on `payments/stripe.ts`. - `shortcuts/keymap.ts:18` has a switch with one case per action, separate from the menu's list. - `ui/CommandPalette.tsx:55` keeps its own list of actions, and it's missing the newer ones. - `ui/SettingsDialog.tsx:61` sets a global `skipRefocus` flag to stop the logout dialog it opens from sending focus to the message input. - `history/undo.ts:30` has a special case for every action that can be undone. - `refunds/refund.ts:22` wraps every Stripe call in `if (order.provider === "paypal")`. - Every action handler has to call `track()` by hand, and some don't. - `ui/Toolbar.test.tsx` and `ui/Menu.test.tsx` test the same actions separately. ``` Then with the fixes: ```md - Make the general `Dialog` give focus back to whatever had it before it opened, so the wait and the flag can both go. - `ui/LogoutDialog.tsx:30` waits 100ms after closing and hopes the message input can take focus by then. - `ui/SettingsDialog.tsx:61` sets a global `skipRefocus` flag to stop the logout dialog it opens from sending focus to the message input. - Define a `PaymentProvider` interface that Stripe and PayPal both implement, so checkout and refunds no longer know which on

card.purpose_zh: 对代码库做一次彻底重构，让智能体每次改动读得更少、更少无声破坏、调试更快；以目标方式执行到结束，并可选清理注释与测试。
does: 先列出可选的注释清理与测试清理，询问用户选择后只做所选部分
不改代码，先通读代码库并记录隐藏耦合、无谓耦合、冗余与特殊分支等问题
从第一性原理重新设计修复方案，把每个修复写在它解决的问题之上
按清单实施全部修复，移除重设计后不再需要的特殊分支
若选了测试，最后处理测试：删除重复实现、绑定内部、永不失败的测试
用子代理反复检查四类问题，直到没有值得修复的问题为止
inputs: 可选：要聚焦的区域或关注点（argument-hint）
用户对是否清理注释、是否清理测试的选择
outputs: 问题清单与修复方案组成的决策日志
清理后的注释与测试（若用户选择）
scenarios: 代码库结构混乱、改动常引发意外破坏时
希望减少智能体每次改动所需阅读量时
需要统一分散在多处的重复逻辑与动作列表时
调试困难、根因难定位时
重构前需要系统性梳理依赖方向时
prerequisites: 代码库可被智能体读取与修改
用户需先回答是否做注释清理与测试清理
limits: 原文未说明支持的具体语言或框架
重构后行为应与开始时一致，仅允许顺带修复的缺陷
完成标准依赖子代理检查，原文未给出量化阈值
注释与测试清理为可选，需用户明确选择
